title: ABA Formal Opinion 471: Ethical Obligations of Lawyer to Surrender Papers and Property to which Former Client is Entitled
author: ABA Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion addresses former-client file surrender, retention, and document-sharing duties under Model Rules 1.15 and 1.16(d). It does not discuss legal AI, task-level capability, verification of AI output, selective deployment, or AI-driven operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Document stewardship: Digital files preserve professional duties
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s proposition that professional file-stewardship duties extend to electronic records. It establishes an end-product minimum, requires otherwise internal materials when necessary to protect an unfinished matter, encourages sound document-management arrangements, and expressly limits its scope to ethical duties rather than broader property rights.

kp.k: Opinion establishes ethical duties, not property rights
kp.d: The Committee interprets ABA Model Rules governing file transfer after representation ends; it does not address AI. Its scenario concerns a municipality replacing its lawyer after a ten-year contractual relationship and requesting all open and closed files. Because the lawyer has been paid in full, retaining liens are outside the opinion's scope. The Committee cautions that jurisdiction-specific law and rules may impose other obligations.
qs: The opinion does not address a client’s property rights or other legal rights to these materials.
A lawyer has represented a local municipality for 10 years pursuant to a contract for legal services.
Because the lawyer has been paid in full, this opinion does not address retaining liens.
There may be other obligations defined in a jurisdiction’s case law or court rules.

kp.k: Termination requires protecting clients and returning their property
kp.d: Under Model Rules 1.15 and 1.16(d), lawyers must safeguard client property, deliver it promptly on request, and take reasonably practicable steps to protect clients when representation ends. Absent other law or a valid Rule 1.15(e) dispute, the municipality must receive all property it supplied, including original documents. These are ethical requirements rather than empirical findings.
qs: Model Rule 1.15 provides that a lawyer must safeguard a client’s property and promptly deliver it to the client upon the client’s request.
This would necessarily include original documents provided by the client.
These steps include, but are not limited to, “surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled.”

kp.k: Jurisdictions differ between entire-file and end-product approaches
kp.d: The Committee reports that a majority of jurisdictions follow an entire-file approach: lawyers must surrender representation-related materials unless they establish an exception. Reported exceptions include confidentiality duties to others, assessments of the client, safety risks, and internal firm communications or assignments. Other jurisdictions distinguish deliverable end products from preparatory materials that need not automatically be surrendered.
qs: A majority of jurisdictions follow what is referred to as the “entire file” approach.

In those jurisdictions, at the termination of a representation, a lawyer must surrender papers and property related to the representation in the lawyer’s possession unless the lawyer establishes that a specific exception applies and that certain papers or property may be properly withheld.

These variations distinguish between documents that are the “end-product” of a lawyer’s services, which must be surrendered and other material that may have led to the creation of that “end-product,” which need not be automatically surrendered.

kp.k: Committee reaffirms end-product approach as ethical minimum
kp.d: The Committee affirms its 1977 opinion as the Model Rules' minimum, subject to circumstances requiring additional disclosure. For the municipality, required materials include client-supplied items, filed or filing-ready legal documents, executed instruments, tribunal records, relevant correspondence, discovery and exhibits, requested legal opinions, and paid third-party assessments or records.
qs: The Committee affirms the position taken in Informal Ethics Opinion 1376 as it states the minimum required by the Rules.
However, there may be circumstances in individual representations that require the lawyer to provide additional materials related to the representation.
legal documents filed with a tribunal - or those completed, ready to be filed, but not yet filed;
legal opinions issued at the request of the municipality; and
third party assessments, evaluations, or records paid for by the municipality.

kp.k: Internal work materials generally need not be surrendered
kp.d: On the stated facts, particularly for concluded matters, the Committee generally excludes materials generated primarily for the lawyer's internal purposes. Examples include drafts, internal research and memoranda, conflict checks, personal notes, hourly billing statements, firm assignments, ethics-consultation notes, client assessments, and documents potentially revealing other clients' confidences. This is qualified by the separate duty to protect clients in unfinished matters and by jurisdictional requirements.
qs: In contrast, under these facts, it is unlikely that within the meaning of Rule 1.16(d), the client is entitled to papers or other property in the lawyer’s possession that the lawyer generated for internal use primarily for the lawyer’s own purpose in working on the municipality’s matters.
This is particularly true for matters that are concluded.
internal legal memoranda and research materials;
documents that might reveal the confidences of other clients.

kp.k: Unfinished matters can require disclosing internal drafts and research
kp.d: Client protection can override the ordinary exclusion of internal work. The Committee requires disclosure where internal notes or memoranda have no final product and withholding them would harm the municipality's interests. Its concrete example is an imminent filing deadline: the most recent draft and relevant supporting research should pass to the former client.
qs: In this fact scenario, if the lawyer has materials that are: (1) internal notes and memos that were generated primarily for the lawyer’s own purpose in working on the municipality’s matter, (2) for which no final product has emerged, and (3) the materials should be disclosed to avoid harming the municipality’s interest, then the lawyer must also provide the municipality with these materials.

For example, if in a continuing matter a filing deadline is imminent, and as part of working on the municipality’s matter the lawyer has drafted documents to meet this filing deadline, but no final document has emerged, then the most recent draft and relevant supporting research should be provided to the municipality.

kp.k: Electronic records fall within client-file obligations
kp.d: The opinion expressly extends file-related obligations to electronic materials. It recognizes technological changes in creating, communicating, using, and storing client materials, but does not decide when lawyers must convert electronic files to paper or who pays conversion costs. It endorses reasonable lawyer-client agreements governing file maintenance, delivery formats, and associated costs.
qs: This obligation exists with respect to all materials whether in paper or electronic form.
The use of the term “paper” in Rule 1.16(d) includes all communications noted above, whether tangible or electronic.

Lawyers and clients may enter into reasonable agreements addressing how the client’s files will be maintained, how copies will be provided to the client if requested, and who will bear what costs associated with providing the files in a particular form; entering into such agreements is prudent and can help avoid misunderstandings.

kp.k: Document retention depends on professional judgment and substantive importance
kp.d: The Committee does not comprehensively determine which materials must initially be retained or how long closed files must be preserved. It links retention and safeguarding to competence and diligence, varying with each representation. It contrasts typically dispensable logistical emails with likely necessary settlement-offer communications and recommends good document-management policies. It also observes that drafts can offer clients relatively little value while imposing preservation and cataloguing burdens.
qs: Thus, drafts and other documents representing work by a lawyer are often of relatively small value to clients and can be burdensome for a lawyer to preserve, catalogue, and maintain.

In general, a lawyer’s ethical obligation to retain and safeguard material relating to a representation arises pursuant to a lawyer’s duties of competence and diligence and will depend on the facts and circumstances of each representation.
By contrast, the lawyer likely would need to retain an email to the client in which the lawyer communicates and evaluates a settlement offer from an opposing party.
Consistent with duties under the Model Rules, lawyers are encouraged to develop good document management policies.

kp.k: Prior delivery does not settle final file-transfer duties
kp.d: The Committee encourages regular provision of information and documents during representation and advising clients to retain them. Nonetheless, having supplied copies previously does not determine whether they must be supplied again at termination. The opinion recommends explaining copying-cost responsibility and applicable circumstances in retainer letters.
qs: The Committee encourages lawyers to regularly provide clients with information and copies of documents during the course of the matter and encourages lawyers to advise clients to maintain these documents.

The fact that copies of certain materials may have been previously provided to a client is not dispositive of whether the lawyer must also provide such materials at the termination of a representation.
Lawyers are encouraged to explain in their retainer letters who is responsible for the costs of copying and under what circumstances.
